Elements
ĕl´ĕ-mĕnts
n. pl. (first principles, rudiments; also the constituent stuff of the heavens — Greek stoicheia)
Latin elementum, a first principle. The Greek stoicheia means things in a row — the ABC, the rudiments; and by extension the basic constituents of the physical order.

Biblical Definition

Elements renders a Greek word meaning rudiments — the ABC of a subject — and Paul uses it of the state of the church before Christ came. “Even so we, when we were children, were in bondage under the elements of the world” (Gal 4:3). The old covenant order of days, months, times and years was a schoolmaster: real, God-given, and elementary. To return to it after Christ is therefore not conservatism but regression: “now, after that ye have known God, or rather are known of God, how turn ye again to the weak and beggarly elements, whereunto ye desire again to be in bondage?” (Gal 4:9). The adjectives are severe — weak, because ceremonies cannot justify; beggarly, because they have nothing left to give once the substance has come. Peter uses the same word of the physical creation at the end: “the day of the Lord will come as a thief in the night; in the which the heavens shall pass away with a great noise, and the elements shall melt with fervent heat, the earth also and the works that are therein shall be burned up” (2Pe 3:10), and again, “the heavens being on fire shall be dissolved, and the elements shall melt with fervent heat” (2Pe 3:12). The rudiments of religion are outgrown in Christ; the elements of the world are dissolved at His coming.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines element as the first or constituent principle of any thing; the simplest part; and in the plural, the rudiments or first principles of any art or science.

expand to see more

EL'EMENT, n. The first or constituent principle or minutest part of any thing.

2. An ingredient; a constituent part of any substance.

3. In the plural, the first rules or principles of an art or science; rudiments.

RU'DIMENT, n. A first principle or element; that which is to be first learnt.

Key Scripture

Galatians 4:3 — "Even so we, when we were children, were in bondage under the elements of the world:"

Galatians 4:9 — "But now, after that ye have known God, or rather are known of God, how turn ye again to the weak and beggarly elements, whereunto ye desire again to be in bondage?"

2 Peter 3:10 — "But the day of the Lord will come as a thief in the night; in the which the heavens shall pass away with a great noise, and the elements shall melt with fervent heat, the earth also and the works that are therein shall be burned up."

2 Peter 3:12 — "Looking for and hasting unto the coming of the day of God, wherein the heavens being on fire shall be dissolved, and the elements shall melt with fervent heat?"

Modern Corruption

The ceremonies Christ fulfilled are reimposed as marks of seriousness, and the promised dissolution of the present order is quietly dropped as embarrassing.

expand to see more

Galatians 4 is aimed at people who thought they were advancing. They were adding observances, taking on discipline, becoming more rigorous — and Paul says they were turning again to weak and beggarly elements and desiring to be in bondage. The pattern recurs whenever a church treats ceremony, calendar, dietary rule or ascetic practice as the mark of a serious Christian. Those things were the alphabet; Christ is the language. To go back to the alphabet after learning to read is not devotion. Paul's alarm in this epistle — I am afraid of you, lest I have bestowed upon you labour in vain — is proportioned to what is at stake, which he says elsewhere is falling from grace.

Second Peter 3 is dropped for the opposite reason: it is too concrete. The heavens passing away with a great noise, the elements melting with fervent heat, the earth and its works burned up — this is not the language of a symbol, and it is regularly softened into one. Peter draws two conclusions and neither is speculative. First, since all these things shall be dissolved, what manner of persons ought ye to be in all holy conversation and godliness. Second, we look for new heavens and a new earth wherein dwelleth righteousness. The dissolution is not the end of the story; it is the clearing of the ground.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek stoicheia (G4747), rudiments, first principles, and the constituent elements of the world — Galatians 4:3, 4:9, Colossians 2:8, 2:20, Hebrews 5:12, 2 Peter 3:10, 3:12.

expand to see more

Greek stoicheion (G4747) — a rudiment or element; Galatians 4:3 and 4:9, Colossians 2:8 and 2:20, Hebrews 5:12, 2 Peter 3:10 and 3:12.

Greek ptochos (G4434) — beggarly, destitute; Galatians 4:9, of the elements returned to.

Greek luo (G3089) — to loose, dissolve; 2 Peter 3:10-12 of the elements melting.

Hebrews 5:12 uses the word of the first principles of the oracles of God, which the readers needed taught again.

The same word covers the ABC of religion and the constituent stuff of the heavens; both are provisional.

Usage

"“In bondage under the elements of the world” — the alphabet, before the language."

"“How turn ye again to the weak and beggarly elements?”"

"“The elements shall melt with fervent heat” — and then, what manner of persons ought ye to be."
